items.evidence_note: Randomised trial in sports-active adults with patellar tendinopathy.

summary: 52 sports-active adults with patellar tendinopathy were randomised to 3 vs 1 exercise session per week for 12 weeks.
VISA-P improved in both groups, but extended restitution was not better than short restitution.
Pain and strength also improved, while tendon structure did not.
The primary outcome was self-reported, so blinding limits certainty a little.

items.bottom_line: In this single-centre RCT, 12 weeks of exercise-based rehab improved VISA-P, pain, and strength in both groups, but adding more rest between sessions did not add benefit over three sessions per week.

methods.setting: Bispebjerg and Frederiksberg Hospital, Copenhagen, Denmark.
methods.participants: 52 sports-active adults aged 18–60 years with patellar tendinopathy.

results.result: No group or interaction effect; both groups improved.
results.detail: Mean VISA-P rose from 55.9 to 68.3 in the SR group and from 48.8 to 63.9 in the ER group. The paper reports no significant group effect (p = 0.16) and no interaction effect (p = 0.54).

results.result: Pain on activity, daily activity, rest, and decline squat fell in both groups.
results.detail: The paper reports significant time effects for pain during physical activity, daily activity, rest, and single-leg decline squat, with no group or interaction effects for the pain measures used for the main comparison.

results.result: Peak torque increased in both groups.
results.detail: The paper reports a significant time effect for maximal isokinetic peak torque, with no group or interaction effect.

FNB + SNB lowered 24 h opioid use vs control; donor-site infiltration combinations ranked well for pain.
At 48 h and for PONV, comparative estimates were imprecise or null.
Authors judged the network heterogeneous and did not formally grade certainty with GRADE or CINeMA.

pico.i: Regional or local analgesic techniques, alone or combined
pico.c: Placebo, blank control, systemic analgesia, or another block
pico.o: Pain, opioid use, time to first analgesic request, PONV

limits: Sparse network for some comparisons.
Clinical heterogeneity and transitivity were uncertain.
Functional outcomes were not synthesised.

items.bottom_line: This review suggests some regional or local techniques can improve early pain after ACL reconstruction, especially when donor-site analgesia is added, but the size and durability of benefit are uncertain and no single block is clearly superior.

methods.design: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of RCTs
methods.setting: Adults having ACL reconstruction under general anaesthesia
methods.participants: 31 RCTs; 2,470 patients; mean age 24.0 to 35.1 years across studies
methods.intervention: Regional and local analgesic techniques, including ACB, FNB, LIA, iPACK, ONB, SNB, and combinations
methods.comparator: Placebo, blank control, systemic analgesia, or another regional/local technique
methods.primary_outcome: 24 h oral morphine milligram equivalents; pain, TFAR, and PONV were also main outcomes

results.result: FNB and FNB+SNB were lower than control; all other comparisons had CrIs crossing 0.
results.detail: The review reports lower estimated opioid use for these two comparisons only; it does not report an MCID for OMME.

results.result: ACB+donor-site infiltration was lower than ACB and some LIA comparisons; most others crossed 0.
results.effect: ACB+donor-site infiltration vs ACB MD -1.23 (-2.38 to -0.01)
results.detail: The paper cites about 1 point on a 0-10 VAS as an MCID reference for acute postoperative pain, but this interval includes values smaller than that threshold.

results.result: ACB+donor-site infiltration was lower than ACB, control, FNB, and LIA; other comparisons mostly crossed 0.
results.effect: ACB+donor-site infiltration vs ACB MD -1.50 (-2.43 to -0.61)
results.detail: The point estimate exceeds the paper’s 1-point VAS reference, yet the interval also includes effects smaller than 1 point.
The review found no clear comparative advantage at 48 h, despite SUCRA rankings.

results.result: ACB, FNB, and LIA had shorter TFAR than ACB+iPACK; others crossed 0.
results.effect: ACB vs ACB+iPACK MD -7.50 (-13.01 to -1.92); FNB -7.80; LIA -8.42
results.meaning: Possible longer time to rescue with ACB+iPACK
results.detail: No MCID was reported for TFAR, and the authors say it should be interpreted with background analgesia and rescue criteria in mind.

how_to_apply: Expect the largest early analgesic signal from combinations that cover more pain sources.
Do not treat SUCRA rankings as proof of a clinically best block.
Be cautious with 48 h pain claims; the review found no clear comparative differences.
Interpret opioid use and TFAR alongside rescue-analgesia protocols.
applies_to: Adults having ACL reconstruction under GA

weaknesses: Network was sparse for several nodes.
Clinical heterogeneity and transitivity were uncertain.
No formal GRADE or CINeMA certainty assessment.
Functional outcomes and harms were limited.

grade.reason: Most included trials had some concerns or high risk, and sensitivity analyses changed several estimates after excluding high-risk studies.
Heterogeneity varied and some comparisons showed moderate to high heterogeneity, although global inconsistency was small.
Comparisons mixed different graft types, protocols, and block variants, so transitivity was uncertain.
Several key CIs crossed 0, and even positive pain effects included values below the paper’s 1-point VAS reference.
The review found no clear small-study effects, though power was limited for smaller networks.

clinical_significance: The review uses about 1 point on a 0-10 VAS as the acute postoperative pain MCID reference.
The 24 h VAS estimate of -1.50 is compatible with a clinically worthwhile effect, but the CI reaches -0.61, so a smaller effect remains plausible.
The 48 h pain results do not show a clear clinically meaningful advantage.
No MCID was reported for OMME or TFAR.
comparator_fairness: Controls ranged from placebo to systemic analgesia and other blocks, so some comparisons were more credible than others.
Background and rescue analgesia varied across trials, which can dilute or exaggerate differences.
Some comparisons were likely not balanced for expectation or co-intervention intensity.
alternative_explanations: Natural recovery after surgery could explain part of the pain drop over time.
Regression to the mean may help with early pain outcomes.
Different background and rescue analgesia could drive opioid and TFAR differences.
Differential attrition was less likely because the review says missing data risk was generally low, but selective reporting remained a concern.
spin: The abstract and conclusion are cautious overall and do not claim a single best technique.
Ranking language could still overstate certainty if read without the wide CrIs and sensitivity analyses.
The discussion appropriately tempers the ranking findings with uncertainty.
fit_with_evidence: The authors say the opioid-sparing finding for FNB+SNB is consistent with Hussain et al. 2023.
The review extends earlier ACLR analgesia reviews by adding newer trials and 48 h pain.
Its caution about ranking over certainty fits the broader playbook for ACLR analgesia.
external_validity: Adult ACLR patients under GA are close to a sports-physio caseload after knee ligament surgery.
Mean age was young, mostly 24.0 to 35.1 years, which fits a typical ACLR population.
The evidence comes from multiple countries and mixed hospital settings.
Technique details, graft types, and background analgesia varied, so direct transfer to one local protocol is limited.
would_change_my_mind: A large, well-reported RCT with functional outcomes and consistent rescue protocols would strengthen the case.
A head-to-head trial showing a clear, durable clinical gain at 24 to 48 h with preserved function would matter most.
A formal GRADE/CINeMA assessment showing high certainty across the main comparisons would also strengthen confidence.

items.patient_explanation: Some nerve or local anaesthetic combinations can lower pain after ACL reconstruction, especially in the first day. The benefit is not the same for every technique, and the best option depends on pain source, movement goals, and possible leg weakness.
open_questions: Which technique best preserves early function?
Do donor-site blocks improve rehab outcomes, not just pain?
Which comparisons remain when high-risk trials are removed?
key_findings: 31 RCTs; 2,470 patients.
FNB+SNB reduced 24 h opioid use vs control.
ACB+donor-site infiltration had the best 24 h pain estimate.
48 h pain and PONV remained uncertain.

items.title: Deep and superficial dry needling looked similar for neck pain
items.evidence_note: One full-text triple-blind RCT in neck pain.
items.confidence_note: Full text reported the design, outcomes and main contrasts clearly.
items.impact_line: Tell patients deep needling was not clearly better than superficial needling for pain or disability here.
summary: 44 adults with non-specific neck pain and upper trapezius MTrPs were randomised 1:1 to deep or superficial dry needling.
Pain and disability improved in both groups, but between-group differences were not significant at 2 or 6 weeks.
A Week 6 active RMS contrast favoured deep needling, but it was nominal and exploratory.
Deep needling caused more bleeding and needling-related pain than superficial needling.

pico.p: Adults with non-specific neck pain and upper trapezius myofascial trigger points
pico.i: Deep dry needling, 4 sessions over 2 weeks
pico.o: Ultrasound, sEMG, pain and Neck Disability Index at 2 and 6 weeks

limits: No sham or untreated control.
Multiple outcomes without multiplicity adjustment.
Actual superficial insertion depth was not instrumentally verified.
Single hospital in Saudi Arabia.
Pain duration and comorbidity rates differed numerically at baseline despite non-significant tests.
items.condition: Non-specific neck pain with upper trapezius myofascial trigger points
items.bottom_line: Deep and superficial dry needling both coincided with less pain and disability, but this trial did not show clear superiority of deep needling. The only between-group signal was a nominal Week 6 active RMS difference, which was exploratory.

methods.design: Triple-blind two-arm parallel-group randomised clinical trial
methods.participants: 44 adults with non-specific neck pain and upper trapezius active MTrPs
methods.intervention: Four sessions of deep dry needling over 2 weeks
methods.comparator: Four sessions of superficial dry needling over 2 weeks
methods.primary_outcome: Ultrasonography and sEMG outcomes; pain and disability were secondary

results.detail: Both groups improved from baseline. The confidence interval crosses no effect and a clinically important benefit.
Both groups improved. The confidence interval crosses no effect and does not support a meaningful between-group difference.
Both groups improved, but the between-group CI is wide and crosses no effect.
The CI includes no effect and a potentially important difference in either direction.
This nominally favoured deep needling, but the paper says it was exploratory and no multiplicity adjustment was used.

how_to_apply: Use either technique if the goal is symptom relief; this trial did not show deep needling was better.
If you choose deep needling, warn about more bleeding and needling pain.
Do not promise superior pain relief from deeper penetration based on this study.
Treat the active-RMS finding as hypothesis-generating only.
applies_to: Two sessions per week for 2 weeks
not_for: Claims that deep needling is superior for pain or disability
